title: Machine learning generates active daunomycin-binding synthetic nucleic-acid polymers outside selected sequence families
summary: The study combined in-vitro selection with a conditional variational autoencoder trained on selection data to generate high-affinity highly functionalized nucleic-acid polymer (HFNAP) sequences. Experimentally generated CVAE sequences bound daunomycin with reported dissociation constants of 9–26 nM despite having no apparent primary-sequence similarity to experimentally selected polymers; competition selections found selected generated variants performed as well as or better than sequences obtained after multiple rounds of high-stringency selection.
ai_technology: Conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) trained on in-vitro selection-derived HFNAP sequence/fitness data
organization: Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; Harvard University; Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Brigham and Women's Hospital

evidence.tested: Experimentally generated CVAE sequences bound daunomycin with reported dissociation constants of 9–26 nM despite having no apparent primary-sequence similarity to experimentally selected polymers; competition selections found selected generated variants performed as well as or better than sequences obtained after multiple rounds of high-stringency selection.
evidence.unknown: The finding is target binding by synthetic HFNAPs, not therapeutic efficacy or cellular activity. Binding results are specific to daunomycin and reported assays; the authors describe sequences as having no apparent similarity rather than proving wholly unrelated functional mechanisms. Some competition performance was assessed by in-vitro selection rather than a clinical or organism-level test.
evidence.ai_role: The authors used the CVAE to condition generation of novel HFNAP sequences on predicted daunomycin-binding fitness, then synthesized/tested generated sequences in binding and competition-selection assays. The machine-learning model generated the active sequences; wet-lab selection and competition assays established their binding activity.
